title: Multi‐Proxy Evidence for Environmental Perturbations During the Paleocene‐Eocene Thermal Maximum Record on the Southern Tethyan Shelf
content:
Abstract

The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM, ∼56 Ma) was characterized by a profound carbon cycle perturbation and extreme global warming. However, its environmental impacts on shallow marine settings—particularly the subtropical southern Tethyan shelf—remain inadequately constrained. Here we present integrated organic carbon isotope (δ13CTOC), total organic carbon (TOC) content, and elemental proxies alongside lithological data from the Hanadi section (Egypt) to reconstruct environmental responses across the PETM. Our results suggest that the PETM onset featured accelerated silicate weathering and increased detrital influx under humid conditions. The PETM main body is characterized by a negative carbon isotope excursion (CIE) of ∼4.5‰ in the δ13CTOC, shifting from a pre-excursion value of ∼ −25.0‰ to a minimum of ∼ −29.5‰, which coincides with peak TOC content, and elevated P2O5 content under suboxic-anoxic conditions. We interpret this co-occurring enrichment in TOC and P2O5 as evidence of increased primary productivity and organic carbon preservation. Specifically, efficient phosphorus regeneration may have fueled high productivity and enhanced organic carbon burial—representing a key negative feedback for CO2 drawdown. These findings are consistent with regional patterns observed on the southern Tethyan shelf and in several other locations. However, they contradict with scenarios that are dominated by either prolonged terrestrial weathering or deep-ocean carbonate accumulation, suggesting spatially heterogeneous Earth system responses across the PETM event. Our study thus highlights the role of redox-controlled phosphorus recycling on subtropical southern Tethyan shelf in promoting elevated productivity and organic carbon burial, offering a deep-time perspective on coastal vulnerability under future warming.
